title: unless; as long as; provided
subtitle: unless you are a member / as long as you promise / provided (that) you have somewhere to park
summary: Use unless (= except if) and as long as / so long as / provided / providing (= on condition that) to talk about conditions, with a present tense for the future.

lesson.heading: unless = except if
lesson.text: The club is for members only. You can't go in **unless** you are a member. This means: you can't go in except if you are a member, or you can go in only if you are a member. **Unless** = except if.

examples.text: I'll see you tomorrow **unless** I have to work late.
examples.note: = except if I have to work late

examples.text: There are no buses to the beach. **Unless** you have a car, it's difficult to get there.
examples.note: = except if you have a car

examples.text: *A:* Shall I tell Lisa what happened? *B:* Not **unless** she asks you.
examples.note: = tell her only if she asks you

examples.text: Ben hates to complain. He wouldn't complain about something **unless** it was really bad.
examples.note: = except if it was really bad

examples.text: We can take a taxi to the restaurant - **unless** you'd prefer to walk.
examples.note: = except if you'd prefer to walk

lesson.heading: unless or if ... not
lesson.text: Instead of **unless** it is often possible to say **if ... not**. The meaning is the same.

examples.text: **Unless** we leave now, we'll be late. or **If we don't** leave now, we'll be late.

lesson.heading: as long as / so long as
lesson.text: You can say **as long as** or **so long as** (= if, on condition that). It introduces a condition that must be true.

examples.text: You can borrow my car **as long as** you promise not to drive too fast. or ... **so long as** you promise ...
examples.note: = You can borrow my car, but you must promise not to drive too fast. This is a condition.

lesson.heading: provided (that) / providing (that)
lesson.text: You can also say **provided (that)** or **providing (that)**. The meaning is the same as as long as: but only if.

examples.text: Travelling by car is convenient **provided (that)** you have somewhere to park. or ... **providing (that)** you have ...
examples.note: = It's convenient but only if you have somewhere to park.

examples.text: **Providing (that)** the room is clean, I don't mind which hotel we stay at. or **Provided (that)** the room is clean ...
examples.note: = The room must be clean, but otherwise I don't mind.

lesson.heading: Talking about the future
lesson.text: When we are talking about the future, we do not use will after **unless / as long as / so long as / provided / providing**. We use a present tense.

examples.text: I'm not going out **unless it stops** raining.
**Providing the weather is** good, we're going to have a picnic tomorrow.
examples.wrong: providing the weather will be good

lesson.text: Unless means 'except if' - the sentence is true in every case but one. As long as / provided mean 'only if' - the sentence is true in one case only.

exercises.prompt: You can borrow my car ___ you promise not to drive too fast.
exercises.explanation: This is a condition that must be true (only if you promise), so: as long as.

exercises.prompt: We're going to the beach tomorrow ___ the weather is bad.
exercises.explanation: We're going except if the weather is bad: unless.

exercises.prompt: We're going to the beach tomorrow ___ the weather is good.
exercises.explanation: We're going only if the weather is good: providing (or provided / as long as).

exercises.prompt: Listen carefully, or you won't know what to do. You won't know what to do ___.
exercises.explanation: Unless = except if: You won't know what to do unless you listen carefully.

exercises.prompt: You have to speak very slowly, or he won't understand you. He won't understand you ___.
exercises.explanation: He won't understand you unless you speak very slowly (= except if you speak very slowly).

exercises.prompt: Business must improve soon, or the company will have to close. The company will have to close ___.
exercises.explanation: Use a present tense after unless for the future: unless business improves soon.

exercises.prompt: Don't worry about the dog. It will chase you only if you move suddenly. Say this with unless.
exercises.answer: The dog won't chase you unless you move suddenly.
exercises.explanation: Only if you move suddenly = unless you move suddenly.

exercises.prompt: Today is a public holiday. The doctor will see you only if it's an emergency. Say this with unless.
exercises.answer: The doctor won't see you unless it's an emergency.
exercises.explanation: The doctor won't see you unless it's an emergency (= except if it's an emergency).

exercises.prompt: Match the beginnings and endings of the sentences.

pairs.right: unless I have to work late.
provided you have somewhere to park.
as long as you promise not to drive too fast.

pairs.left: I don't mind which hotel we stay at
We can take a taxi to the restaurant

exercises.prompt: Which word fits the gap: unless, or as long as / provided?

items.text: I don't mind if you come home late ___ you come in quietly.
I'm going now ___ you want me to stay.
I don't watch TV ___ I have nothing else to do.
Children are allowed to use the swimming pool ___ they are with an adult.
___ they are with an adult, children are not allowed to use the swimming pool.
Our holiday cost a lot of money. - Well, that doesn't matter ___ you enjoyed yourselves.

exercises.statement: I'm not going out unless it will stop raining.
exercises.explanation: I'm not going out unless it stops raining. After unless we use a present tense for the future, not will.

exercises.statement: Providing the weather is good, we're going to have a picnic tomorrow.
exercises.explanation: Correct. Providing (that) + present tense is right for a future condition.
